title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator – O₂ Sensor Errors / Low or Unstable FiO₂
description: Troubleshooting guide for O₂ sensor errors, low FiO₂ readings, or unstable oxygen delivery on the Puritan Bennett 980 ventilator using a logical external-first approach.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: If the ventilator is alarming for low FiO₂ and the patient is connected, immediately assess the patient. Confirm SpO₂ and clinical stability. If oxygen delivery is questionable, transfer the patient to another ventilator or manual resuscitation device with verified O₂ source before continuing troubleshooting. Patient safety always comes first.

steps.title: Verify Oxygen Wall Source
steps.instructions: Confirm the oxygen hose is firmly connected to the wall outlet and ventilator inlet. Check that the wall outlet is active and labeled correctly. Listen for gas flow and confirm normal pipeline pressure (typically ~50 psi in most facilities). Swap to a known-good wall outlet if unsure. Low or unstable pipeline pressure can cause inaccurate FiO₂ readings or O₂ supply alarms.

steps.title: Inspect the High-Pressure O₂ Hose
steps.instructions: Check for kinks, cracks, or loose fittings. Swap the hose with a known-good hose if available. Ensure DISS fittings are tight and not cross-threaded. A leaking or partially restricted hose can cause fluctuating FiO₂ readings.

steps.title: Confirm Air Supply
steps.instructions: Verify compressed air is connected and at proper pressure. Loss of air supply can cause incorrect blending and FiO₂ instability. The ventilator blends air and oxygen. If one source is unstable, FiO₂ readings will be unstable.

steps.title: Check for Active O₂ Sensor Calibration Alerts
steps.instructions: Navigate to the ventilator’s sensor or calibration menu. Determine whether the error is calibration overdue, sensor drift, or sensor failure. If calibration is required, follow on-screen calibration procedure using room air or 100% O₂ as instructed. Ensure gas sources are stable during calibration. O₂ sensors naturally drift over time and require periodic calibration.

steps.title: Inspect the O₂ Sensor Module
steps.instructions: Confirm the sensor is properly seated and connected. Check for moisture contamination or condensation. Inspect for physical damage or corrosion at the contacts. If the sensor is replaceable, install a known-good O₂ sensor and perform calibration after replacement. Do not attempt internal board-level repair.

steps.title: Check for Excessive Moisture in the System
steps.instructions: Inspect water traps and expiratory filters. Look for heavy condensation in tubing near the sensor pathway. Replace saturated filters if needed. Moisture contamination can cause inaccurate O₂ readings.

steps.title: Verify Alarm Behavior
steps.instructions: Document the exact alarm message. Determine whether FiO₂ is reading consistently low or fluctuating. Compare displayed FiO₂ to analyzer readings (if available). Note any unusual noises or gas flow irregularities. Using an external oxygen analyzer (if available) can help confirm whether the issue is sensor-related or actual delivery-related.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator alarming ‘O₂ Sensor Error’ with low FiO₂ reading at 40% despite 60% setting.
CCR.Cause: Found O₂ pipeline hose leaking at DISS fitting. FiO₂ unstable due to fluctuating oxygen pressure.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced high-pressure O₂ hose, verified 50 psi pipeline pressure, recalibrated O₂ sensor. FiO₂ stabilized and passed operational check.

helpfulDetails: Final device status (Returned to Service or Sent to Repair)

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator – Flow Sensor Errors / Inaccurate Volumes
description: Troubleshooting guide for flow sensor errors and inaccurate volume readings on the Puritan Bennett 980 ventilator, focusing on external causes before internal failure.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Move the patient to another ventilator if needed. Do not troubleshoot flow sensor issues while actively ventilating a patient unless clinically cleared. Flow measurement errors can directly affect delivered volumes.

steps.title: Verify the Correct Circuit Is Installed
steps.instructions: Confirm adult vs. pediatric circuit matches ventilator configuration. Confirm the circuit type selected in the ventilator settings matches the physical circuit. Incorrect circuit selection can result in inaccurate volume calculations and flow sensor alarms.

steps.title: Inspect the Flow Sensor Placement
steps.instructions: Confirm the proximal flow sensor is installed in the correct orientation. Ensure arrows (if present) align with flow direction. Verify it is securely seated and fully connected. Loose or reversed sensors commonly cause flow sensor errors.

steps.title: Check for Moisture or Condensation
steps.instructions: Inspect the flow sensor for visible moisture. Check the circuit for water accumulation. Drain water traps if present. Replace the flow sensor if contaminated. Moisture alters flow measurement and is one of the most common causes of inaccurate volumes.

steps.title: Inspect the Patient Circuit for Leaks
steps.instructions: Check all connections (wye, humidifier, filters, HME, expiratory limb). Inspect for cracked tubing or loose fittings. Confirm the exhalation valve assembly is properly seated. Leaks can cause volume discrepancies and false flow alarms.

steps.title: Perform a System Check / Calibration
steps.instructions: Remove the patient from the circuit. Perform a full ventilator self-test or extended system check. Ensure calibration completes without error. This allows the ventilator to recalibrate internal flow measurement baselines.

steps.title: Replace the Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: If errors persist, install a new, known-good flow sensor. Re-run system check. Disposable sensors are consumables and can drift or fail over time.

steps.title: Evaluate Alarm Behavior
steps.instructions: Document exact alarm message. Document intermittent vs. constant behavior. Document whether measured tidal volume matches set volume. Document any trending discrepancies. Consistent error after external checks may indicate internal sensing hardware or signal processing issues.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator displaying ‘Flow Sensor Error’ and reported tidal volumes lower than set volume during use in ICU.
CCR.Cause: Moisture observed inside proximal flow sensor. System check initially failed calibration. Sensor replaced and circuit drained.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced proximal flow sensor, drained condensation from circuit, performed full system check. Calibration passed and volume readings returned to normal. Ventilator returned to service.

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator Fails Pre-Use Check / Circuit Leak Detected
description: Troubleshooting guide for Puritan Bennett 980 ventilator failing pre-use check due to circuit leak detection, focusing on external causes before internal pneumatic failure.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is not connected to a patient. Ensure the ventilator is disconnected from the patient before performing any troubleshooting. Leak tests should only be performed with a test lung.

steps.title: Verify Correct Circuit Type Selection
steps.instructions: Confirm that the selected circuit type in the ventilator settings matches the actual circuit installed (adult, pediatric, single limb vs dual limb). A mismatch can cause the ventilator to interpret normal compliance as a leak.

steps.title: Inspect Circuit Assembly from Ventilator to Test Lung
steps.instructions: Check for loose connections at the inspiratory and expiratory ports. Check for partially seated tubing. Check for missing or cracked adapters. Check for improperly installed expiratory filters. Remove and firmly reseat each connection one at a time. Many leaks are caused by incomplete connections.

steps.title: Check the Test Lung and Port Cap
steps.instructions: Ensure the test lung is intact (no tears or loose fittings). Ensure the patient wye is securely attached. Ensure any unused ports are capped. A cracked test lung or open sampling port will trigger a leak failure.

steps.title: Inspect the Humidifier Setup (If Installed)
steps.instructions: If a humidifier is in line, confirm the chamber is properly seated. Check that water chamber seals are intact. Inspect for cracks in the chamber. Ensure temperature probe ports are capped if unused. Temporarily bypass the humidifier with a dry circuit if necessary to isolate the issue.

steps.title: Examine the Expiratory Filter and Valve Area
steps.instructions: Ensure the expiratory filter is installed correctly. Ensure it is not cross-threaded. Ensure it is not damaged. Ensure it is fully tightened. A misaligned filter or debris at the seal can cause leak detection during self-test.

steps.title: Check for Cracked or Worn Tubing
steps.instructions: Run your hand along the tubing and visually inspect for small splits near connectors. Inspect for stress cracks. Inspect for loose swivel joints. Swap with a known-good circuit if available to rule out disposable component failure.

steps.title: Repeat Pre-Use Check After Corrections
steps.instructions: After reseating connections or replacing components, rerun the pre-use check. If the ventilator passes, return it to service.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator failed pre-use check with ‘Circuit Leak Detected’ alarm in ICU prior to patient use.
CCR.Cause: Loose connection identified at expiratory filter housing. Filter not fully seated, allowing leak during self-test.
CCR.Resolution: Reseated expiratory filter, verified tight seal, reran pre-use check. Ventilator passed all tests and returned to service.

helpfulDetails: Whether a known-good circuit was tested
Final device status (Passed pre-use / Sent to repair)

title: Puritan Bennett 840 - Flow Sensor Errors or Calibration Failure
description: Guide for troubleshooting flow sensor errors or calibration failures on Puritan Bennett 840 ventilators.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Move the patient to an alternative ventilator if actively connected. Do not perform troubleshooting while a patient is on the ventilator.

steps.title: Check Power and Connections
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is properly powered and on a stable AC source or fully charged battery. Verify all circuit connections, including the flow sensor assembly, are fully seated and free from damage.

steps.title: Inspect the Flow Sensor
steps.instructions: Remove and visually inspect the flow sensor for moisture, condensation, or debris. Check for cracks, loose components, or signs of contamination that could impede airflow measurement.

steps.title: Verify Circuit Assembly
steps.instructions: Reattach the flow sensor ensuring proper orientation per manufacturer markings. Inspect patient circuit tubing for kinks, obstructions, or misaligned components that may trigger false errors.

steps.title: Perform Calibration
steps.instructions: Initiate the ventilator’s automatic flow sensor calibration procedure. Ensure the sensor is at room temperature and dry; environmental extremes can prevent proper calibration.

steps.title: Check for Software or Settings Issues
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator software version is current and matches hospital standards. Verify any flow compensation or calibration offsets are correctly configured.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator displays flow sensor error and fails calibration.
CCR.Cause: Observed debris in flow sensor and/or misaligned circuit connections preventing calibration.
CCR.Resolution: Cleaned or replaced flow sensor, reattached circuits properly, recalibrated ventilator. If errors persisted, removed ventilator from service and sent for repair.

helpfulDetails: Flow sensor inspected for moisture or debris.
Circuit tubing checked for kinks or disconnections.
Calibration attempts and environmental conditions recorded.

title: Puritan Bennett 840 - Exhalation Module Replacement and Errors
description: Guide for Clinical Engineering to troubleshoot and replace exhalation module errors on Puritan Bennett 840 ventilators, emphasizing patient safety and stepwise resolution.

steps.title: Verify Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is not actively supporting a patient before troubleshooting. If connected, switch the patient to a backup ventilator.

steps.title: Power and Alarm Status Check
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is powered on and no general system errors exist. Note any specific exhalation module alarms or codes.

steps.title: Inspect the Exhalation Module
steps.instructions: Check for visible contamination, damage, or obstruction. Ensure module is fully seated and locked in place according to the manufacturer’s guidance.

steps.title: Disconnect and Re-seat Module
steps.instructions: Power down ventilator if safe. Remove the exhalation module carefully and inspect connectors. Reinsert module, ensuring correct alignment and secure connection.

steps.title: Run Ventilator Self-Test/Calibration
steps.instructions: Power on ventilator. Initiate the self-test or calibration sequence. Observe if module errors persist.

steps.title: Check Related Components
steps.instructions: Inspect patient circuit and expiratory limb for kinks or obstructions. Ensure filters are clean and properly seated.

steps.title: Replace Module if Necessary
steps.instructions: If errors persist, install a verified, clean, and compatible exhalation module. Re-run ventilator self-test to confirm resolution.

CCR.Complaint: Exhalation module errors displayed; ventilator alarms.
CCR.Cause: Module misaligned and/or contaminated; self-test failed.
CCR.Resolution: Module removed, cleaned, and re-seated; self-test run and passed. Replaced module when errors persisted; device verified operational.

title: Puritan Bennett 840 - Pre-use Check Failures
description: Guide for troubleshooting Puritan Bennett 840 ventilators that fail pre-use checks, focusing on external causes and safe escalation.

steps.title: Ensure Safe Environment
steps.instructions: Confirm ventilator is powered off and not connected to a patient. Remove any circuit, tubing, or accessories that could interfere with testing. Why: Pre-use checks must be performed without patient attachment to ensure safety.

steps.title: Check AC Power and Battery
steps.instructions: Verify AC power is connected and outlet is functional. Confirm the internal battery has sufficient charge for a pre-use check. Swap outlet or use a verified power strip if unsure. Why: Power instability can cause pre-use check errors.

steps.title: Inspect Circuit and Connectors
steps.instructions: Remove and reattach all patient circuits, sensors, and tubing. Check for visible cracks, kinks, moisture, or contamination in circuits. Ensure sensors (O₂, flow, pressure) are properly seated. Why: Loose or damaged circuits often cause pre-use check failures.

steps.title: Check the Exhalation Module
steps.instructions: Ensure module is properly installed and free from obstructions. Look for dust, moisture, or buildup that could prevent proper calibration. Why: A misaligned or contaminated exhalation module can prevent successful pre-use checks.

steps.title: Run Environmental and Sensor Verification
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is in a room with ambient temperature and humidity within spec. Remove unnecessary magnetic or electrical interference nearby. Why: Extreme environmental conditions can trigger sensor errors during self-test.

steps.title: Power Cycle and Retry Pre-Use Check
steps.instructions: Power off, wait 30 seconds, and power on. Run the pre-use check following standard prompts. Observe the exact error message and which step fails. Why: Power cycling often clears minor electronic faults.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator fails pre-use check; unable to start ventilation.
CCR.Cause: Pre-use check failed due to exhalation module misalignment and sensor connection issues.
CCR.Resolution: Verified power, reconnected circuits, reseated exhalation module, re-ran pre-use check successfully; ventilator cleared for service.

helpfulDetails: Error messages and failed pre-use check steps noted
Final device status (ready or out of service)

title: Puritan Bennett 840 - Internal Battery Degradation
description: Guide to troubleshoot and manage internal battery degradation in Puritan Bennett 840 ventilators, ensuring patient safety and proper escalation.

steps.title: Verify Power Source
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is connected to a verified working AC outlet or hospital-grade power supply. Confirm indicator lights show AC power is present. Why: Some battery faults appear as battery degradation when the device is actually not charging due to external power issues.

steps.title: Check Battery Charge Status
steps.instructions: Navigate to the ventilator's battery status menu. Record current charge percentage and estimated backup time. Why: Confirms whether the battery is holding charge and if degradation is gradual or sudden.

steps.title: Inspect Battery Connection
steps.instructions: Power off the ventilator. Remove and reseat the internal battery, ensuring all connectors are secure. Why: Loose connections can mimic battery degradation symptoms.

steps.title: Perform Battery Test (if available)
steps.instructions: Run the built-in battery test function. Note any warnings or failures reported by the ventilator. Why: Provides manufacturer-recommended evaluation of battery health.

steps.title: Observe Ventilator During AC Power Loss Simulation
steps.instructions: Only if safe: disconnect AC power and ensure backup battery maintains operation for the expected duration. Why: Confirms real-world battery performance.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator battery backup only lasts ~10 minutes and battery warning displayed.
CCR.Cause: Observed internal battery capacity below manufacturer specifications; battery fails internal test and cannot maintain power during AC disconnect simulation.
CCR.Resolution: Ventilator removed from service, labeled Out of Service, and sent for authorized battery replacement.

helpfulDetails: Battery test results and backup duration.
Any error messages displayed during testing.

title: Puritan Bennett 840 - Compressor Failure or Inadequate Pressure
description: Troubleshooting guide for Puritan Bennett 840 ventilators experiencing compressor failure or inadequate pressure delivery.

steps.title: Verify Power and Electrical Connections
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator is plugged into a working, properly grounded outlet. Check the power cord for visible damage. Why: Inadequate voltage can reduce compressor output or prevent startup.

steps.title: Check for Alarms or Error Messages
steps.instructions: Observe the ventilator display for specific pressure, flow, or compressor-related alarms. Document any error codes for reference. Why: This helps determine if the issue is detected by internal monitoring.

steps.title: Inspect Circuit and Patient Tubing
steps.instructions: Ensure all inspiratory and expiratory tubing is properly connected and free of kinks. Check for any leaks at connections, humidifiers, or filters. Why: Leaks or obstructions can mimic compressor failure by preventing adequate pressure delivery.

steps.title: Evaluate Filters and External Components
steps.instructions: Inspect and replace bacterial/HEPA filters if clogged. Verify the oxygen source or air supply line is functional. Why: Restricted airflow can reduce effective pressure output.

steps.title: Run a Manual or Pre-Use Test
steps.instructions: Execute the ventilator’s built-in leak and pressure tests. Observe if the system can reach target pressures without a patient connected. Why: Confirms whether the problem is device-related or patient-circuit-related.

steps.title: Listen and Observe Compressor Operation
steps.instructions: With the ventilator on, listen for unusual sounds (straining, failure to start, or irregular tone). Observe pressure waveforms on the display. Why: Audible or visual cues can help identify mechanical failure.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator failing to achieve set inspiratory pressures; alarms triggered.
CCR.Cause: External inspection revealed no tubing leaks; filters clear; compressor produces abnormal noise during test.
CCR.Resolution: Ventilator removed from service, labeled Out of Service, and sent for manufacturer repair.

helpfulDetails: Final device status: Out of Service

title: Puritan Bennett 560 - Turbine Failure or Insufficient Flow
description: This guide assists Clinical Engineering in troubleshooting Puritan Bennett 560 ventilators experiencing turbine failure or insufficient airflow.

steps.title: Check Power Supply
steps.instructions: Verify the ventilator is properly plugged into a verified working outlet. Confirm the power switch is ON and the unit completes its startup sequence. Why: Turbine motors rely on consistent power; low or interrupted power can reduce airflow.

steps.title: Inspect Air Intake and Filters
steps.instructions: Remove and inspect the air intake filter for blockage or excessive dust. Clean or replace filters as necessary. Why: Restricted airflow to the turbine can reduce delivered flow and trigger low-flow alarms.

steps.title: Check Circuit and Tubing Connections
steps.instructions: Ensure patient circuit, inspiratory, and expiratory tubing are correctly connected and not kinked. Verify that humidifiers or inline filters are not clogged. Why: Mechanical restrictions in the breathing circuit can mimic turbine failure.

steps.title: Observe Turbine Operation
steps.instructions: Listen for abnormal turbine sounds (grinding, excessive vibration). Ensure the turbine spins freely when running a self-test. Why: Noise or vibration can indicate mechanical wear or impending turbine failure.

steps.title: Run Ventilator Self-Test or Diagnostic Mode
steps.instructions: Follow the ventilator prompts to perform a full self-test. Document any flow or turbine-related errors. Why: The self-test can confirm whether the turbine motor or sensors are functioning properly.

steps.title: Check Environmental Conditions
steps.instructions: Ensure ambient temperature is within the operating range. Remove any dust or obstruction around the ventilator’s air intake. Why: Overheating or restricted airflow around the unit can reduce turbine efficiency.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator delivering insufficient flow; alarms triggered; turbine suspected.
CCR.Cause: Air intake filter partially blocked; tubing unobstructed; turbine self-test indicates error code 12 (turbine malfunction).
CCR.Resolution: Replaced air filter and ran diagnostic; issue persists. Device labeled Out of Service and sent for repair.

helpfulDetails: Tubing and circuit checked for obstructions
Self-test results and error codes documented
Turbine noise or unusual vibration observed

title: Puritan Bennett 560 - Battery Not Charging or Shortened Runtime
description: Guide for troubleshooting battery issues on Puritan Bennett 560 ventilators, including failure to charge and shortened runtime.

steps.title: Verify AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is connected to a working outlet. Test the outlet with a known working device. Why: A non-functional outlet or loose connection will prevent charging.

steps.title: Inspect Power Cord and Connections
steps.instructions: Check for frayed cables, broken connectors, or loose plugs. Ensure the cord is fully seated in both the ventilator and outlet. Why: Damaged or loose cords prevent proper power delivery.

steps.title: Check Battery Seating
steps.instructions: Remove the battery and reseat it according to manufacturer instructions. Ensure locking mechanism engages fully. Why: Improperly seated batteries may not charge or provide full runtime.

steps.title: Observe Ventilator Indicators
steps.instructions: Check charging LED or screen battery icon for status. Note any error messages related to battery or power. Why: Indicators can reveal whether the device recognizes the battery.

steps.title: Test with Spare/Service Battery
steps.instructions: If available, replace the battery with a known good unit. Observe charging behavior and runtime. Why: Confirms if the original battery is degraded or defective.

steps.title: Allow Full Charge Cycle
steps.instructions: Connect the battery to AC power for the recommended charging time. Monitor if the battery reaches full charge and maintains it. Why: Short or interrupted charge cycles may give the appearance of failure.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator battery not charging and provides only 10 minutes of runtime.
CCR.Cause: Battery seated correctly but fails to accept charge; LED indicates low battery despite AC power.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced battery with known good unit; device charges and holds runtime as expected. Original battery labeled for replacement/repair.

title: Puritan Bennett 560 - Circuit Disconnect Alarms
description: Guide for troubleshooting circuit disconnect alarms on Puritan Bennett 560 ventilators, focusing on external causes before internal faults.

steps.title: Verify Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Ensure the patient is stable and ventilated by another device or manual ventilation if needed. Never troubleshoot an active patient on the affected ventilator.

steps.title: Check Circuit Connections
steps.instructions: Inspect all tubing connections from the ventilator to the patient. Ensure inspiratory and expiratory limbs are properly seated. Confirm humidifier, filters, and adapters are correctly installed. Loose or misaligned connections are the most common cause of disconnect alarms.

steps.title: Inspect for Leaks or Damage
steps.instructions: Check the circuit for cracks, holes, or kinks. Ensure all ports on the ventilator and patient interface are sealed. Replace any damaged tubing or connectors.

steps.title: Verify Flow Sensors and Adapters
steps.instructions: Inspect the flow sensor, if used, for proper placement and cleanliness. Make sure any D-lite or patient adapters are seated correctly.

steps.title: Check Ventilator Settings
steps.instructions: Confirm the ventilator mode matches the circuit configuration (e.g., single limb vs. dual limb). Ensure tidal volume and alarms are appropriately set.

steps.title: Power Cycle the Ventilator
steps.instructions: Turn the ventilator off and back on to clear false alarms after verifying the circuit is intact.

steps.title: Observe Alarm Behavior
steps.instructions: If alarms persist, note whether they occur immediately upon connection or intermittently during operation. Document any unusual sounds, leaks, or error codes.

CCR.Complaint: User reports repeated “circuit disconnect” alarms while ventilating patient.
CCR.Cause: Loose expiratory limb connection and kinked inspiratory tubing observed during inspection.
CCR.Resolution: Reconnected tubing securely, replaced damaged sections, verified circuit integrity, ventilator returned to service.

helpfulDetails: No unusual sounds, heat, or odor detected

title: Puritan Bennett 560 - Pre-use Self-test Failures
description: Guide to troubleshoot Puritan Bennett 560 ventilators that fail pre-use self-test, focusing on external factors before internal failure.

steps.title: Verify Power Source
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is connected to a functional AC outlet. Check that the power cord is fully seated. Why: Inadequate power can cause self-test failure or incomplete initialization.

steps.title: Check Battery Status
steps.instructions: Confirm the internal battery has sufficient charge. If battery is low, allow charging or replace with a known good battery. Why: Low battery can prevent successful self-test completion.

steps.title: Inspect Circuit and Connections
steps.instructions: Ensure patient circuit is correctly attached, no kinks, leaks, or loose connections. Verify sensors, flow sensors, and pressure lines are properly seated. Why: Disconnects or leaks often trigger self-test failures.

steps.title: Confirm Environmental Conditions
steps.instructions: Ensure ambient temperature and humidity are within manufacturer specifications. Remove any obstructions near air intakes or exhausts. Why: Extreme conditions can affect turbine performance and self-test.

steps.title: Reset the Ventilator
steps.instructions: Power down, wait 30 seconds, and power back on. Run the self-test again. Why: Sometimes a simple reset resolves minor electronic glitches.

steps.title: Swap Known Good Accessories
steps.instructions: Replace patient circuit, flow sensors, or connectors with verified functional units. Why: External components can cause false test failures.

steps.title: Check for Active Alarms or Error Logs
steps.instructions: Review any messages displayed during self-test. Document alarm codes for reference or escalation. Why: Error codes can indicate specific sensors or components causing failure.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator fails pre-use self-test; displays error codes and will not enter clinical service.
CCR.Cause: External verification showed patient circuit disconnected and low battery. All accessories reseated, power verified, environmental conditions normal.
CCR.Resolution: Ventilator reset and self-test rerun after reconnections. If failure persists, removed from service and labeled Out of Service for repair.

helpfulDetails: Final device status (operational or Out of Service)

title: Puritan Bennett 560 - Oxygen Sensor Errors
description: Guide for troubleshooting oxygen sensor errors on PB560 ventilators, ensuring accurate FiO₂ delivery and patient safety.

steps.title: Verify power and device readiness
steps.instructions: Ensure the ventilator is powered on and has passed its basic self-test. Confirm that any pre-use check screens are clear before proceeding. Why it matters: Sensor errors can sometimes be falsely reported if the device is in a transitional state or not fully initialized.

steps.title: Inspect the oxygen sensor physically
steps.instructions: Locate the oxygen sensor (typically near the inspiratory limb or inside the sensor module). Check for obvious damage, contamination, or moisture on the sensor tip. Ensure it is securely seated in its connector. Why it matters: Loose or contaminated sensors are the most common cause of errors.

steps.title: Check connections and wiring
steps.instructions: Verify that the sensor cable is not frayed, bent, or pinched. Disconnect and reconnect the sensor to confirm a solid connection. Why it matters: Poor connections can cause intermittent readings or trigger error codes.

steps.title: Review sensor calibration status
steps.instructions: Check the ventilator menu for sensor calibration status. If the sensor requires calibration or replacement, note the date of last calibration. Why it matters: Some sensors have a limited life and must be recalibrated to function properly.

steps.title: Swap with a known good sensor (if available)
steps.instructions: Replace the current sensor with a functioning spare. Observe if the error persists. Why it matters: Confirms whether the issue is with the sensor itself or the ventilator electronics.

steps.title: Verify FiO₂ delivery and readings
steps.instructions: Run a test on the ventilator with the patient circuit disconnected (ensure patient safety). Observe the oxygen concentration readings for stability and accuracy. Why it matters: Helps ensure the ventilator reports accurate oxygen levels before patient use.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator shows oxygen sensor error during pre-use check.
CCR.Cause: Sensor cable was loose, or sensor tip contaminated (observed during inspection).
CCR.Resolution: Reconnected the sensor securely and cleaned the sensor tip. Tested ventilator; error resolved. If unresolved, note sensor replacement or device sent to service.

helpfulDetails: Sensor serial number and installation date

title: Puritan Bennett 840 Ventilator - Alarm: AC POWER LOSS Operating on battery
description: Troubleshooting guide for the AC POWER LOSS Operating on battery alarm on the Puritan Bennett 840 Ventilator, indicating loss of AC input and risk of shutdown if external power is not restored.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Immediately confirm the patient is being ventilated adequately. Prepare backup ventilation such as a manual resuscitator or alternate ventilator if needed. Do not allow troubleshooting to interrupt patient support.

steps.title: Verify the Reported Alarm and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm the AC POWER LOSS alarm is active. Check that the ventilator indicates battery operation, the AC power indicator is off, the audible alarm is present, and any battery runtime countdown is displayed.

steps.title: Check AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Verify the outlet supplying the ventilator is active using a known-good device. Confirm connection to the correct hospital-grade or emergency power outlet if applicable.

steps.title: Inspect Power Cord and Connections
steps.instructions: Ensure the AC power cord is firmly seated at both the wall outlet and the ventilator. Inspect for cuts, fraying, or loose connectors, then reseat the cord securely.

steps.title: Check Power Strip or Extension Use
steps.instructions: If the ventilator is connected through a power strip or extension, bypass it and plug directly into the wall outlet. Verify any intermediate device is powered on and functioning.

steps.title: Verify Facility Power Availability
steps.instructions: Check nearby equipment for power, confirm whether the outlet is on emergency power, and ask staff if there was a recent localized or broader power interruption.

steps.title: Observe for AC Power Recovery
steps.instructions: After correcting the external power source, confirm the AC power indicator turns on, verify the ventilator returns to AC power, and ensure the alarm clears automatically.

steps.title: Remove from Service if Alarm Persists
steps.instructions: If AC power is confirmed at the outlet and all external causes have been ruled out but the ventilator remains on battery, remove the device from service, label it Out of Service, and send it for repair or bench evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator alarmed AC POWER LOSS and switched to battery operation during patient use.
CCR.Cause: AC power source was unavailable or the power cord connection at the wall outlet was loose, preventing AC input to the ventilator.
CCR.Resolution: Reseated the power cord, confirmed outlet functionality, verified return to AC power, and confirmed the alarm cleared. Device returned to service after normal operation was verified.

title: Puritan Bennett 840 Ventilator - Alarm: LOW AC POWER mains power below acceptable level
description: LOW AC POWER alarm indicating insufficient mains voltage leading to battery use, unstable operation, or risk of ventilator shutdown

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Transfer patient to backup ventilator if needed and confirm continuous ventilation.

steps.title: Verify Alarm and Behavior
steps.instructions: Confirm alarm presence, observe power indicators, and check for battery switching.

steps.title: Check AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Test outlet with known-good device and try alternate verified outlet.

steps.title: Inspect Power Cord
steps.instructions: Ensure secure connections and check for damage or wear.

steps.title: Check Power Distribution
steps.instructions: Remove extension cords and plug directly into wall outlet.

steps.title: Verify Voltage Configuration
steps.instructions: Confirm correct voltage setting in service mode.

steps.title: Observe for Resolution
steps.instructions: Confirm alarm clears and unit remains on stable AC power.

CCR.Complaint: Ventilator alarming LOW AC POWER; unit intermittently switching to battery during use
CCR.Cause: Verified stable wall power and connections; alarm persisted indicating likely internal power supply issue

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator - Will Not Power On or Fails During Startup
description: Troubleshooting no-power conditions, blank displays, interrupted startup, repeated rebooting, startup alarms, or failure to reach the normal ventilator setup screen.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a Puritan Bennett 980 that will not start or complete startup while it is connected to a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team immediately. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Provide manual ventilation when clinically required and directed by qualified clinical staff. Confirm proper ventilation, oxygen delivery, and alarm operation on the replacement equipment. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on a ventilator that cannot complete its startup sequence. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the affected PB980 has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: Confirm the Exact Failure
steps.instructions: Attempt to identify and document whether the ventilator: Shows no lights, sounds, fans, or display activity. Powers the breath delivery unit but not the graphical user interface. Begins startup and then shuts down. Reboots repeatedly. Stops at a specific startup screen. Displays a technical fault, diagnostic code, or failed self-test message. Produces an alarm tone without completing startup. Observe both the graphical user interface and the status display on the breath delivery unit. The PB980 incorporates a separate status display that can provide additional indication of ventilator operation. Expected outcome: The failure is narrowed to total power loss, display-related behavior, interrupted startup, or a reported system fault.

steps.title: Inspect for Immediate Safety Hazards
steps.instructions: Before reconnecting power, inspect the ventilator for: Liquid intrusion or evidence of a spill. Damaged casing, wheels, or mounting hardware. A crushed, cut, burned, or frayed power cord. Bent or damaged power-plug blades. Unusual heat, smoke, odor, discoloration, or arcing. Blocked cooling vents or excessive dust accumulation. Evidence that the ventilator was dropped or struck. Do not energize the unit when liquid intrusion, burning odor, smoke, severe physical damage, or electrical damage is present. Expected outcome: No immediate electrical, fire, or mechanical hazard is found. If a hazard is present, stop troubleshooting, remove the ventilator from service, and send it for controlled bench evaluation.

steps.title: Verify the AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Disconnect the ventilator and test the wall receptacle with an approved outlet tester or another known-good device. Confirm that: The receptacle provides the correct facility voltage. The outlet is not controlled by an unexpected wall switch. The circuit breaker or isolated-power system has not tripped. The receptacle retains the plug securely. The outlet is approved for critical-care equipment. Avoid relying solely on the report that “the outlet works.” Expected outcome: The AC source is verified as functional and appropriate. If the outlet fails testing, move the ventilator to a verified receptacle. If the ventilator then starts normally, stop and document the facility power problem.

steps.title: Inspect and Reseat the Power Cord
steps.instructions: Disconnect AC power and inspect the full length of the power cord. Confirm that the plug is fully inserted into the wall outlet. Confirm that the equipment-end connection is fully seated and secured. Look for looseness, exposed conductors, damaged insulation, bent contacts, or heat discoloration. Verify that the cord has not been pulled partially free by bed movement, transport, or equipment positioning. Replace a removable suspect cord only with an approved, known-good equivalent. Expected outcome: The ventilator has a secure, undamaged connection to verified AC power. If reseating or replacing the cord restores normal startup, complete the required operational and safety checks before returning the unit to service.

steps.title: Disconnect Nonessential External Accessories
steps.instructions: Power the ventilator off and disconnect nonessential external devices, including: USB devices. Network or data cables. Remote alarm or nurse-call cables. External displays or communication accessories. Nebulizer accessories. Other optional peripheral connections not required for basic startup. Leave only the approved power connection and equipment necessary for a controlled startup evaluation. Expected outcome: An external accessory or damaged peripheral connection is ruled out as a cause of startup interruption. If the ventilator starts normally, reconnect accessories individually to identify the device or cable associated with the failure. Stop using the suspect accessory.

steps.title: Check Battery and AC-Power Indications
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator to verified AC power and observe all available indicators. Determine whether: The AC-power indicator illuminates. A battery indicator appears. The breath delivery unit status display becomes active. The graphical user interface remains blank. The unit operates only from battery or only from AC. The ventilator immediately shuts down when AC power is removed. The PB980 supports battery operation, but battery availability must not be treated as proof that the AC input or internal charging system is functioning correctly. Medtronic describes the PB980 as using hot-swappable batteries, depending on configuration. Expected outcome: Clinical Engineering determines whether incoming AC power, stored battery power, or both are being recognized. Do not repeatedly cycle power from a severely depleted or questionable battery.

steps.title: Allow Adequate AC Charging Time When the Battery Is Depleted
steps.instructions: If the ventilator has been stored, unplugged, or unused for an extended period: Connect it directly to a verified AC receptacle. Confirm that an AC or charging indication is present. Allow the battery to charge according to facility procedure and the applicable manufacturer documentation. Attempt startup again after sufficient charging time. Do not assume a fully depleted battery is the only problem if the ventilator also fails to respond while connected to verified AC power. Expected outcome: A deeply discharged battery condition is either corrected or ruled out. If the ventilator starts after charging, evaluate battery condition and runtime before returning the unit to clinical use.

steps.title: Perform One Controlled Power Cycle
steps.instructions: If no electrical hazard is present: Turn the ventilator off. Disconnect AC power. Allow the unit to remain fully powered down briefly. Reconnect it directly to a verified AC receptacle. Turn it on using the normal power control. Observe the complete startup sequence without repeatedly pressing controls. Record: Which displays illuminate. Whether fans or pneumatic components activate. Any alarm tones. The last screen or message displayed. Any diagnostic or technical fault code. Whether the failure occurs at the same point each time. Expected outcome: A temporary startup state clears, or the failure becomes repeatable and documentable. If the ventilator completes startup normally, continue with all required pre-use testing before considering it operational.

steps.title: Verify the Graphical User Interface Connection Externally
steps.instructions: Inspect the graphical user interface, mounting arm, and externally accessible cable path without removing covers. Check for: A loose or visibly damaged external cable. Pinching at the mounting arm or pivot points. Evidence of impact damage. A powered breath delivery unit with a completely blank graphical interface. Intermittent display activity when the unit or arm is positioned normally. Do not open the graphical user interface or breath delivery unit during basic troubleshooting. Expected outcome: Obvious external display-connection damage is identified or ruled out. A working breath delivery unit status display with an inactive graphical interface may indicate a display, cable, communication, or internal power problem requiring bench evaluation.

steps.title: Record Startup Messages and Diagnostic Codes
steps.instructions: Photograph or transcribe any startup message exactly as displayed. Document: Full fault wording. Diagnostic code. Date and time. Software version, when visible. Whether the fault clears or repeats. Whether the failure occurs on both AC and battery power. The point in the startup sequence where operation stops. Do not clear logs, perform unauthorized software changes, or repeatedly reboot the ventilator in an attempt to bypass a persistent fault. Expected outcome: Repair personnel receive precise information that can be correlated with manufacturer service documentation.

steps.title: Complete Required Testing After a Successful Startup
steps.instructions: A ventilator that eventually starts after an unexplained failure should not immediately be returned to patient use. Complete the facility-approved inspection and applicable manufacturer testing, including: Startup and power-on self-test verification. Short self-test or equivalent pre-use test, as applicable. Alarm verification. AC-to-battery transfer testing. Battery condition and runtime evaluation. Ventilation performance verification with an appropriate test lung and analyzer. Electrical safety testing when the power cord, power source, or electrical integrity was questioned. Review of diagnostic or event information when accessible through approved procedures. Medtronic directs users to the PB980 operator’s manual for complete operating instructions, warnings, and pre-use requirements. Expected outcome: The ventilator consistently starts, passes required testing, and performs normally before being released. If any test fails or startup remains intermittent, remove the ventilator from service.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Puritan Bennett 980 remained blank and would not complete startup when needed for patient use.
CCR.Cause: Verified wall power and power cord were functional, but the ventilator repeatedly stopped during startup with the same technical fault displayed.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the PB980 from service, labeled it Out of Service, documented the startup fault, and routed it for authorized bench evaluation.

Unusual heat, smell, smoke, or sound

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator - Battery Not Charging or Short Runtime
description: Troubleshooting battery charging failures, reduced runtime, unexpected battery depletion, AC power recognition problems, loose connections, aging batteries, or internal charging-system faults.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot a battery or charging problem while the Puritan Bennett 980 is actively supporting a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team that backup battery operation may be unavailable or unreliable. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator using the facility’s approved clinical procedure. Confirm that the replacement ventilator is operating correctly and has adequate backup power. Do not intentionally disconnect AC power while the affected ventilator is supporting a patient. Expected outcome: The patient is no longer dependent on a ventilator with uncertain backup power. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the affected PB980 has been safely removed from patient use. The PB980 is intended for trained healthcare professionals in acute or critical-care environments, making dependable power operation a patient-safety requirement.

steps.title: Confirm the Reported Battery Problem
steps.instructions: Determine whether the issue involves: Battery not charging; Battery charge percentage not increasing; Battery indicator missing or showing an error; Unexpected switch to battery while connected to AC; Battery discharging unusually quickly; Ventilator shutting down shortly after AC power is removed; Failure involving the primary battery, extended battery, or both. Record any displayed alarms, status messages, battery indicators, and the approximate runtime reported by staff. Expected outcome: The exact failure pattern is identified before parts are replaced. If the report cannot be reproduced and all power indications remain normal, document the findings and continue with an operational battery check.

steps.title: Verify the AC Power Source
steps.instructions: Connect the ventilator directly to a known-good hospital-grade receptacle. Avoid extension cords, adapters, switched power strips, and unverified isolation-power outlets. Test the original receptacle with an approved outlet tester or another known-good device. Confirm the receptacle provides stable power and is not controlled by a wall switch. Check whether nearby equipment also experienced a power interruption. Expected outcome: The ventilator recognizes AC power and the battery begins or continues charging. If the battery charges normally from the known-good receptacle, the original outlet or external power source was the likely cause. Stop troubleshooting and address the facility power issue.

steps.title: Inspect the Power Cord and Connections
steps.instructions: Disconnect the ventilator from AC power before inspecting the cord. Check for: Loose connection at the wall receptacle; Incomplete connection at the ventilator; Bent, recessed, contaminated, or damaged connector contacts; Cuts, crushing, exposed conductors, discoloration, or heat damage; A loose plug that falls out of the receptacle; Evidence that the cord has been stretched or repeatedly rolled over. Reconnect the cord firmly at both ends. When approved by facility policy, test with a known-good compatible power cord. Expected outcome: AC power remains continuously recognized without movement-related interruptions. If replacing or reseating the cord restores charging, remove the defective cord from service and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: Confirm AC and Battery Status Indications
steps.instructions: Power the ventilator from the verified AC source and observe the graphical user interface and status display. Confirm that: AC power is recognized; The battery is detected; A charging indication is present when charging is required; No battery, power-system, or charging-related alarm remains active; The charge level does not continue decreasing while connected to AC. Allow enough time to determine whether the displayed charge level is increasing. A severely depleted battery may not show an immediate large percentage change. Expected outcome: The PB980 detects both AC power and the installed battery, and the charge level begins trending upward. If AC power is not recognized despite a verified outlet and cord, stop external troubleshooting and escalate for bench evaluation.

steps.title: Inspect Accessible Battery Installation
steps.instructions: With the ventilator powered down and removed from AC power, inspect the externally accessible battery installation according to facility procedures. Check for: Battery not fully seated or latched; Loose accessible battery connection; Incorrect battery installation; Damaged latch, cover, housing, or connector area; Swelling, cracking, leakage, corrosion, or discoloration; Unusual heat or chemical odor; Missing battery where one is expected. Do not use a swollen, leaking, overheated, cracked, or physically damaged battery. Expected outcome: The battery is correctly installed, mechanically secure, and free from visible damage. If reseating an undamaged battery restores detection and charging, complete the required operational verification and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: Check Battery History and Condition
steps.instructions: Review the equipment history, battery label, installation date, previous work orders, and recent runtime complaints. Look for: Battery age beyond the facility’s approved replacement interval; Long periods of storage without charging; Repeated deep discharge events; Previous battery alarms; Gradual runtime reduction; A recent battery replacement followed by continued charging problems. Battery capacity decreases with age and use. A battery may appear fully charged but lose voltage rapidly when placed under load. Expected outcome: Battery age and service history are consistent with acceptable performance. If the battery is aged, has repeated runtime complaints, or has exceeded the approved replacement interval, replace it with the correct manufacturer-approved battery and complete post-replacement testing.

steps.title: Compare Primary and Extended Battery Behavior
steps.instructions: When the ventilator is equipped with more than one battery, review each battery’s status separately if the interface permits. Determine whether: One battery is detected and the other is missing; One battery charges while the other does not; Both batteries show the same abnormal condition; Runtime improves when a known-good battery is installed in the affected position. Do not interchange batteries or positions unless permitted by the applicable service documentation and facility procedure. Expected outcome: The problem is isolated to a specific battery or shown to affect the ventilator’s complete charging system. If one battery consistently fails while another approved battery functions correctly, replace the defective battery and stop troubleshooting after successful verification.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Charging Check
steps.instructions: Connect the PB980 to verified AC power in a safe bench area. Record the starting battery percentage or status. Allow the ventilator to remain connected for an appropriate charging period. Confirm that AC recognition remains stable. Record whether the battery indication increases. Monitor for battery alarms, abnormal heat, smell, or repeated charging interruptions. Do not cover ventilation openings or leave a battery showing abnormal heat unattended. Expected outcome: Battery charge increases without alarms, excessive heat, or loss of AC recognition. If the battery remains unchanged or continues discharging while AC is continuously recognized, suspect a failed battery or internal charging-system problem.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Runtime Check
steps.instructions: Perform this check only off-patient in a controlled environment and according to facility policy. Begin with a fully charged battery indication. Configure the ventilator with an approved test circuit and test lung. Record the ventilation settings and installed accessories. Disconnect AC power while maintaining close observation. Confirm that the ventilator transfers to battery without interruption. Monitor battery status, alarms, and elapsed operating time. Reconnect AC power before battery exhaustion or at the facility’s defined test endpoint. Runtime depends on battery condition, ventilation settings, accessories, battery configuration, and environmental conditions. Compare the result with the applicable manufacturer specification and facility acceptance criteria rather than relying only on staff estimates. Expected outcome: The ventilator transfers correctly to battery and meets the approved runtime requirement. If the battery depletes prematurely, replace the suspected battery with an approved known-good battery and repeat the test.

steps.title: Test With a Known-Good Approved Battery
steps.instructions: When authorized, install a known-good compatible battery with verified service history. Confirm correct seating and detection. Connect the ventilator to AC and verify charging. Complete a controlled battery transfer and runtime check. Compare the result with the original battery. Expected outcome: A known-good battery charges and provides acceptable runtime. If the known-good battery resolves the issue, replace the original battery and complete all required performance and safety verification. If the known-good battery also fails to charge or provides abnormal operation, suspect the ventilator’s internal charger, battery communication, power-distribution circuitry, wiring, or related electronics.

steps.title: Complete Final Operational Verification
steps.instructions: After correcting the problem: Confirm stable AC operation. Confirm the battery is detected and charging. Confirm transfer from AC to battery occurs without ventilation interruption. Confirm return to AC power is recognized. Verify battery and power alarms using the approved test procedure. Confirm no unusual heat, odor, or noise is present. Verify the ventilator passes the facility’s required functional and electrical-safety testing. Confirm the battery is adequately charged before returning the ventilator to clinical service. Expected outcome: The PB980 operates correctly on AC and battery power and meets the facility’s return-to-service criteria. If all checks pass, return the ventilator to service and document the completed work.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Puritan Bennett 980 displayed a low battery condition and operated for only several minutes after AC power was disconnected.
CCR.Cause: Testing found that the installed primary battery indicated a full charge but lost capacity rapidly under ventilator load; AC input and charging indications were otherwise normal.
CCR.Resolution: Replaced the failed battery with an approved replacement, verified charging, confirmed uninterrupted AC-to-battery transfer, completed a controlled runtime test, and returned the ventilator to service.

helpfulDetails: Unusual heat, swelling, leakage, or odor

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator - Touchscreen or GUI Unresponsive
description: Troubleshooting a frozen, blank, inaccurate, intermittently responsive, or completely unresponsive GUI caused by contamination, software state, power, connections, or display failure.

steps.title: Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot an unresponsive touchscreen or GUI while the Puritan Bennett 980 is actively supporting a patient. Notify respiratory therapy and the clinical team that ventilator controls may be unavailable or unreliable. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator using the facility’s approved procedure. Provide an approved alternative ventilation method when clinically required. Confirm effective ventilation and alarm operation on the replacement device. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on a ventilator whose settings cannot be reliably viewed or changed. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the affected PB980 has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: Confirm the Exact GUI Failure
steps.instructions: Determine whether the problem involves: A completely blank display; A frozen screen with information still visible; Touch input failing across the entire screen; Only one area of the screen not responding; Delayed or intermittent touch response; Incorrect touch location or unintended selections; A display that restarts repeatedly; A display problem occurring only during startup. Observe the separate status display on the breath delivery unit for power, ventilation, alarm, or fault information. The PB980 includes this additional display as a redundant indication of ventilator operation. Expected outcome: The failure is clearly identified as a display, touchscreen-input, startup, or complete ventilator problem.

steps.title: Check for Screen Contamination or Physical Interference
steps.instructions: Inspect the touchscreen for: Moisture; Cleaning residue; Medication or adhesive residue; Heavy fingerprints or oils; Protective film lifting from the surface; Labels or tape contacting the active display area; Cracks, impact damage, or pressure marks. Power the ventilator off before cleaning. Clean the screen only with products and methods approved by the manufacturer and facility policy. Do not spray liquid directly onto the GUI. Allow the screen to dry fully before testing. Expected outcome: The display surface is clean, dry, unobstructed, and free from visible damage. If normal touch operation returns, complete an operational verification and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: Verify That the GUI Is Not Locked or Awaiting Confirmation
steps.instructions: Review the displayed screen for: A control-lock condition; A confirmation prompt; A modal message covering normal controls; A startup or pre-use screen requiring an approved response; A menu or window that must be closed before other controls respond. Attempt to operate several different on-screen controls rather than repeatedly pressing one location. Expected outcome: A screen lock, open prompt, or software-navigation condition is either identified and cleared or ruled out. If the GUI responds normally afterward, verify all critical controls and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: Check External Power and Power Indicators
steps.instructions: Verify: The AC power cord is fully seated at the ventilator and approved outlet. The outlet supplies the correct voltage. The cord and plug have no cuts, bent contacts, heat damage, or looseness. The ventilator’s power and status indicators behave normally. The breath delivery unit status display remains active. Test the outlet with an approved electrical tester or known-good device when permitted. A blank GUI accompanied by loss of all ventilator indicators suggests a broader power problem rather than an isolated touchscreen failure. Expected outcome: Stable external power is confirmed, and the issue is isolated to the GUI or touchscreen when other ventilator indicators remain operational.

steps.title: Inspect the GUI Assembly and External Connections
steps.instructions: With the ventilator powered off and disconnected from the patient: Confirm the GUI is securely mounted. Inspect accessible GUI cables and connectors for looseness, strain, pinching, cuts, or impact damage. Check that cables have not been pulled during transport or caught on the cart. Look for liquid intrusion, damaged connector housings, or bent mounting components. Do not disconnect or reseat internal connectors unless authorized by the service procedure and performed by qualified personnel. Expected outcome: The GUI mounting and externally accessible connections are secure and undamaged. If a loose external connection is found and can be safely corrected without internal disassembly, secure it and retest the ventilator.

steps.title: Perform a Controlled Restart
steps.instructions: Only after the ventilator has been removed from patient service: Turn the ventilator off using the normal shutdown process when the GUI permits. Disconnect AC power. Allow the ventilator to shut down completely. Reconnect it to a verified AC outlet. Start the ventilator and observe the GUI throughout the complete startup sequence. Do not repeatedly cycle power if the GUI continues freezing or restarting. Repeated restarts can obscure an intermittent fault without correcting its cause. Expected outcome: The GUI completes startup, displays information correctly, and responds consistently to touch. If the restart restores operation, continue with functional verification before returning the ventilator to service.

steps.title: Check for Startup Errors, Alarms, or Diagnostic Information
steps.instructions: Record all displayed or status-screen information, including: Diagnostic codes; Technical alarms; POST or startup failures; Repeated reboot behavior; Communication-related messages; Loss-of-GUI indications; Software version, when accessible; Time and circumstances of the failure. Photograph or transcribe the information according to facility policy before restarting the ventilator again. Expected outcome: Available fault information is preserved for repair evaluation and vendor support.

steps.title: Test the Entire Touchscreen
steps.instructions: When the GUI is responsive, test controls across multiple areas of the screen: Upper and lower portions; Left and right sides; Center area; Menu selections; Setting adjustments; Confirmation controls; Alarm-related screens. Watch for: Dead zones; Delayed response; Incorrect selections; Double activation; Intermittent freezing; Touch response without corresponding visual feedback. Do not rely on a touchscreen that works only in certain areas. Expected outcome: The full active touchscreen area responds accurately and consistently. If any dead zone or inaccurate response remains, remove the ventilator from service.

steps.title: Remove External Accessories That May Affect Operation
steps.instructions: Disconnect nonessential external accessories one at a time while the ventilator is powered off, such as: USB devices; External communication cables; Data-interface accessories; Network connections; Nonessential peripheral equipment. Restart and retest after removing questionable accessories. Do not disconnect required gas or breathing-system components during a formal performance test. Expected outcome: An external accessory or communication connection is either identified as the cause or ruled out. If the GUI operates normally after an accessory is removed, inspect or replace that accessory and document the finding.

steps.title: Complete an Operational Verification
steps.instructions: Before returning the PB980 to clinical use: Confirm the GUI remains responsive after extended operation. Verify all touchscreen regions. Confirm displayed settings match selected values. Verify alarm indicators and audible alarms. Complete the manufacturer-required pre-use or short self-test procedures. Test the ventilator with an appropriate test lung. Confirm the breath delivery unit status display agrees with normal ventilator operation. Verify there are no unresolved technical alarms. The manufacturer provides the PB980 operator’s manual and supporting reference materials as the primary instructions for operation and verification. Expected outcome: The ventilator completes required testing with a stable, accurate, and fully responsive GUI. If the issue was resolved but cannot be confidently duplicated or verified, keep the ventilator out of service for further observation or bench evaluation.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory therapy reported that the Puritan Bennett 980 GUI displayed ventilation information but did not respond to touchscreen selections.
CCR.Cause: Touchscreen remained unresponsive after cleaning, verifying AC power, inspecting accessible GUI connections, removing external accessories, and performing a controlled restart.
CCR.Resolution: Ventilator was removed from service, labeled Out of Service, and routed for bench evaluation of the GUI and communication hardware.

helpfulDetails: Entire screen or isolated area affected

title: Puritan Bennett 980 Ventilator - Exhalation System or Expiratory Filter Fault
description: Troubleshooting exhalation-system alarms, expiratory filter restriction, condensate buildup, poor exhaled-volume measurement, abnormal PEEP, or failed exhalation-related SST tests.

steps.title: 1. Ensure Patient Safety First
steps.instructions: Do not troubleshoot an exhalation-system fault while the Puritan Bennett 980 is actively supporting a patient. Transfer the patient to another verified ventilator or approved ventilation method. Confirm effective ventilation, oxygenation, and alarm operation on the replacement equipment. An exhalation restriction or valve problem may interfere with pressure relief, PEEP control, exhaled-volume monitoring, and the patient’s ability to exhale. Expected outcome: The patient is safely supported without relying on the affected ventilator. Continue Clinical Engineering troubleshooting only after the PB980 has been removed from patient use.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the Exact Reported Fault
steps.instructions: Review the alarm message, diagnostic code, event log, and SST history. Determine whether the complaint involves: An exhalation-system or expiratory-filter alarm; Failed SST Exhalation Filter Test; Failed SST Exhalation Valve Performance Test; Elevated expiratory resistance; Abnormal or missing exhaled-volume readings; Inability to maintain the selected PEEP; Unexpected circuit pressure during exhalation; A fault that began after a filter or circuit change. The PB980 SST separately evaluates exhalation-valve performance, expiratory filter or compartment occlusion, circuit resistance, leaks, and pressure sensing. Expected outcome: The specific failure and affected SST test are identified and documented.

steps.title: 3. Inspect the Expiratory Limb
steps.instructions: Disconnect the test circuit and inspect the entire expiratory limb for: Kinked, compressed, or twisted tubing; Condensate in dependent loops; Blocked water traps; Secretions or foreign material; Incorrectly installed adapters; Damaged connectors; Unapproved accessories creating excessive resistance. Replace the circuit or expiratory limb with a known-good compatible assembly when its condition is uncertain. The ventilator may detect expiratory-limb occlusion caused by condensate, secretions, kinked tubing, or excessive downstream resistance. Expected outcome: The expiratory pathway is open, dry, correctly assembled, and free of unnecessary restrictions. If this resolves the fault and the ventilator subsequently passes testing, stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the Expiratory Filter
steps.instructions: Open the exhalation-filter compartment and verify that the correct adult/pediatric or neonatal filter configuration is installed. Inspect the filter for: Moisture saturation; Visible contamination; Discoloration; Cracked housing; Damaged seals; Deformed connectors; Incorrect orientation; Incomplete insertion. Confirm that the filter sits fully in its guides and that the patient-side connection aligns correctly with the filter door. The exhaled-gas pathway passes through the condensate vial, exhalation filter, exhalation flow sensor, and exhalation valve before reaching the exhaust port. Expected outcome: The correct filter is properly installed and shows no evidence of obstruction or damage.

steps.title: 5. Reseat the Filter and Secure the Door
steps.instructions: Remove and reinstall the expiratory filter according to the approved configuration. Confirm that: The filter is fully seated; The condensate vial is properly attached; The filter door closes completely; The exhalation-filter latch is fully lowered; The expiratory circuit connects without side loading or misalignment. The PB980 filter compartment uses a dedicated door and latch to retain the filter assembly. Expected outcome: The assembly is secure, correctly aligned, and sealed.

steps.title: 6. Check the Condensate Vial
steps.instructions: Inspect the vial for accumulated liquid, contamination, cracks, damaged threads, or an incomplete seal. Empty the vial before the liquid reaches the maximum fill line. Reinstall it fully and verify that it reaches its mechanical stop. The manufacturer warns that excessive condensate can enter the ventilator, and removal of the vial may cause pressure loss or a disconnect alarm. Do not drain or remove the vial while the ventilator is connected to a patient. Expected outcome: The vial is empty or below its limit, undamaged, and sealed correctly to the filter.

steps.title: 7. Replace the Expiratory Filter
steps.instructions: Install a known-good, compatible expiratory filter assembly. Use the appropriate configuration for the selected patient category. Do not reuse a disposable filter, substitute an unapproved filter, or attempt to clean a component designated for single use. When replacing a reusable assembly, confirm that it has been processed, inspected, dried, and released according to the manufacturer’s instructions and facility infection-control policy. Expected outcome: The alarm clears or the failed filter-related test passes with the replacement filter. If the replacement filter corrects the problem, document the restricted, wet, damaged, or improperly seated filter as the cause and stop troubleshooting.

steps.title: 8. Inspect the Exhalation Compartment and Exhaust Area
steps.instructions: With the filter removed, visually inspect accessible areas of the compartment without internal disassembly. Look for: Standing liquid; Debris; Damaged guides or latch components; Bent or obstructed mating surfaces; Evidence that fluid entered beyond the condensate vial; Blockage around the ventilator exhaust port; Unusual odor, heat, or signs of contamination. Do not insert tools, compressed air, swabs, or cleaning fluids into internal pressure or flow passages. A blocked exhaust port or excessive resistance at the exhaust can contribute to exhalation-path occlusion. Expected outcome: No external obstruction, liquid intrusion, or physical damage is found. If liquid has entered the ventilator, remove the device from service and escalate for bench evaluation.

steps.title: 9. Install a Known-Good Test Circuit
steps.instructions: Connect a complete known-good circuit, including the correct expiratory filter, condensate vial, humidification configuration, and accessories. Confirm that the selected patient type and circuit configuration match the installed components. Remove unnecessary adapters or accessories that could add resistance. Expected outcome: The external circuit and filter assembly are eliminated as possible causes.

steps.title: 10. Run the Full SST
steps.instructions: Allow the ventilator to reach the required operating condition, then run the complete Short Self Test using the installed test circuit and accessories. Pay particular attention to: SST Exhalation Valve Performance; SST Circuit Pressure Test; SST Leak Test; SST Exhalation Filter Test; SST Circuit Resistance Test; SST Circuit Compliance Test. The Exhalation Filter Test checks for filter and exhalation-compartment occlusion, while the Exhalation Valve Performance test evaluates and calibrates valve behavior. Expected outcome: All SST tests pass without Alert, Override, or Failure status. Do not return the ventilator to service based only on an overridden SST alert. The manufacturer warns that overriding an SST alert may allow operation outside stated accuracy specifications.

steps.title: 11. Perform a Controlled Functional Verification
steps.instructions: After SST passes, connect an approved test lung or ventilator analyzer and verify: Stable delivered pressure; Correct PEEP control; Normal inspiratory and expiratory flow waveforms; Reasonable inspired and exhaled tidal volumes; No unexpected pressure retention during exhalation; No exhalation-system alarms; No abnormal valve noise; No leakage around the filter or condensate vial. Use more than one representative setting when required by facility procedure. Expected outcome: The ventilator completes repeated breaths with stable exhalation, accurate monitoring, and no alarms. If the fault returns, stop testing and escalate.

CCR.Complaint: Respiratory Therapy reported an exhalation-system fault and repeated failure of the PB980 SST Exhalation Filter Test.
CCR.Cause: Inspection found a moisture-saturated expiratory filter and condensate at the maximum fill level, creating excessive expiratory-path resistance.
CCR.Resolution: Removed the ventilator from service, replaced the expiratory filter, emptied and reseated the condensate vial, installed a verified test circuit, and completed SST and functional testing with all results passing.

helpfulDetails: Exact alarm message and diagnostic code
Condensate vial level and seal condition
Water found in the expiratory limb
